Description: Impact of Soil Freeze/Thaw Dynamics on the North American Carbon Cycle.  Changes in frozen ground have great impacts on environment and engineering construction.  There is an increasing need for the general public to understand these impacts and potential consequences under global warming scenarios.  To educate the general public and transfer knowledge of frozen ground to the next generation, the overall objective of this proposal is to assist K-12 students/teachers and the public to understand frozen ground, its relation to climate system and its impact on engineering in cold regions.  The objective will be accomplished through the development and thorough evaluation of an online resource for the education and public audiences. Impacts of Soil FrcezelThaw Dynamics on the North American Carbon Cycle PIs: Tingjun Zhang, Lixin Lu, Kevin Schaefer, and A. Scott Denning We will integrate remote sensing data sets, ground-based measurements, and numerical modeling to quantify the effects of soil temperature, soil freeze-thaw dynamics, and snow cover on seasonal to inter-annual variability in the North American terrestrial carbon cycle. Our overall goal is to understand the role of freeze-thaw processes in determining seasonal and inter-annual variability in terrestrial biomass, photosynthesis, respiration, and net C02 fluxes over continental North America. Using remote sensing products, in situ observations, and a soil thermodynamic model, we will estimate soil temperatures and snow cover over North America at 25-km resolution for North America from 1981-2003 (23 years). We will feed these estimated soil temperatures and snow cover, along with additional remote sensing data, into an ecosystem model to estimate biomass and net carbon fluxes. Both models will use the North American Regional Reanalysis, so the resulting estimates of soil thermodynamic properties, biomass, and carbon ,fluxes will be optimally consistent with each other and with actual weather conditions in North America. We will statistically analyze these optimal carbon fluxes to understand the environmental drivers and biophysical responses regulating the spatial patterns and temporal variability in the North American terrestrial carbon cycle. Using standard Monte Carlo techniques, we will quantify uncertainty in our estimated carbon fluxes. Lastly, we will perturb our input data to assess the sensitivity of our estimated fluxes to long-term climate change. Our research addresses the North American Carbon Program (NACP) goals of reducing uncertainty about the buildup of greenhouse gases in the atmosphere and the dynamics of the carbon cycle. Specifically, we address the NACP goal~ of I) quantifying the magnitudes and distributions of terrestrial carbon sources and sinks within North America; 2) understanding the processes controlling carbon source and sink dynamics; and 3) producing consistent analyses of the carbon budget of North America, explaining regional contributions and year-to-year variability. We will archive data products generated by this investigation at the National Snow and Ice Data Center;,s Frozen Ground Data Center for access by other NACP investigators and for general use by the scientific community.

Description: Understanding Long-Term Changes in the Atmosphere of Neptune and Uranus. We propose to study long-term changes in the detailed chemistry of Neptune's atmosphere, focusing particularly on ethane. Mid-IR spectroscopy reveals abundance variations of this hydrocarbon with timescales that range from decades to days. By employing radiative transfer (RT) modeling, we will determine the ethane abundance and vertical distribution, and thus constrain models of the vertical aerosol distribution in the upper troposphere and lower stratosphere. We will put the variation in the context of known changes (both spatial and temporal) at other wavelengths, focusing in particular on ground-based observations, data from the Voyager Encounter in 1989, and data from the Hubble Space Telescope. The appearance of Uranus at visible, near-IR, and radio wavelengths is changing as the planet approaches its 2007 equinox. Disk-integrated visible and near-IR photometry also suggest aerosol structure variability, leading some to speculate that hydrocarbon abundances may be varying significantly as insolation changes. We will investigate this possibility with atmospheric RT code, and establish new observational constraints on the behavior of the stratosphere of the pre-equinox Uranus based on Voyager data. Because Uranus is so similar to Neptune in pressure, temperature, composition, and observability, it provides an excellent comparative target for outer planet studies. Finally, both these planets appear to be responding to small changes in some solar parameter (using solar irradiance as a proxy). If confirmed, this correlation may have significant implications for studies of solar interaction with the terrestrial atmosphere

Description: THE CATHOLIC UNIVERSITY OF AMERICA UNDERSTANDING FLARES WITH EARLY IMPULSIVE HARD X- RAY EMISSION I propose a comprehensive study of those RHESSI flares in which impulsive hard X-ray emission is seen early in the flare before the soft X-ray emission has risen significantly. Compared to the more normal flares where the soft X-ray emission rises well before the hard X-ray emission, this type of early impulsive flares offers the following significant advantages: (1) Evidence for a low-energy cutoff in the nonthermal electron spectrum can be identified at lower energies in the X-ray spectrum because of the relatively low intensity of the thermal emission. This will allow a more accurate estimate to be made of the total energy in the nonthermal electrons. (2) Absence of a strong thermal source from loops allows the detection of any nonthermal sources in the beginning of flares, which will provide critical information on particle acceleration and transport. (3) Possible mechanisms for filling the loops with heated plasma can be differentiated using the RHESSI soft X-ray images. Chromospheric evaporation appears as filling from below while direct heating of plasma already in the loops or in the current sheet from which the loops are formed appears as filling from above. This study is crucial to understanding energy release and heating mechanisms in flares. (4) A comparative study of the more normal flares will be made to investigate possible causes of the early impulsive flares and the particle acceleration mechanism, and how they might different from the more normal flares. I plan to actively participate in two excellent existing education/outreach programs, one at the Goddard Space Flight Center and one at the Catholic University of America. At Goddard, I will interact with teachers and students of sixth grade and promote a positive attitude in them toward math and science using RHESSI as a vehicle. At the Catholic University, I will be involved with an experimental physical science curriculum for undergraduate, pre-service K-8 science teachers. Solar images and movies from recent space missions including RHESSI will be used to educate the future teachers basic physical science.

Description: "IONIZATION STRUCTURE OF THE STELLAR WIND IN THE HIGH MASS X-RAY BINARY VELA X-1" The high-mass X-ray binary Vela X-l/HD 77581, consisting of a 283 s pulsar/B0.5 lab supergiant, will be observed at five critical phases of the binary orbit (8.96 days) to probe the effects of X-ray photoionization. The pulsar ionizes its surroundings as it moves through the binary orbit, producing X-rays while accreting some of the ambient stellar wind from B0.5 lab supergiant. The FUSE spectra will be used to 1) characterize the phase-dependent X-ray ionization of the stellar wind and its density distribution, including the photoionization wake at 55 = 0.6 - 0.9, 2) study enhanced abundances in the atmosphere of the primary, and 3) search for the 283-s pulsar periodicity in the stellar wind lines. 0 VI 1032-38, S IV 1063-73, and P V 11 18-28 are the primary diagnostics to achieve these objectives. These line profiles are unsaturated across the full velocity range of the stellar wind, resulting in a complete picture of the run of optical depth (or Mw)ith velocity. Strong saturation in the stellar wind lines at longer wavelengths (N V, C IV, Si IV) have precluded such studies. P V is the only unsaturated transition of a dominant ionization stage in the wind, hence it provides a direct measure of the bulk wind properties. Chandra HETGS spectra show the temperature of the X-ray ionized region of the wind is -120,000 K, making 0 VI an excellent diagnostic of this plasma. Our recent Cycle 4 observations of another HMXB system (4U1700-37) demonstrate the power of the FUSE region for studying the effects of the X-ray source on the stellar wind that feeds the accretion.

Description: A Method for Identifying Mineralogical Signatures in Locales with Large Topography using Atmospherically Equalized Themis Data We will develop a method for using THEMIS data to study the mineralogy of surfaces that have large elevation changes, such as the unusual blocky terrain in Melas Chasma, in order to identify locales of mineralogical interest. Surfaces with large topography are commonly difficult to interpret using THEMIS data alone because atmospheric transmittance typically dominates the observed radiance. Fortunately, there is a quasi-linear relationship between topography and transmittance, allowing the quasi-linear effect of transmittance to be characterized and removed, and the mineralogy of surfaces identified. The tasks are to: 1) Study and use the quasi-linear relationship between elevation and transmittance to create a real-time atmospheric correction for THEMIS data, 2) Test the technique at the Valles Marineris and globally, 3) Test the technique for areas with known mineralogy, 4) Use THEMIS and TES data to study areas identified with the equalization technique. We anticipate that the results will allow us to identify and mineralogically characterize small outcrops using the high spatial resolution THEMIS data in and around the Valles Marineris, as well as other regions with large topography on Mars.

Description: "MODEL INVESTIGATIONS OF UPPER-TROPOSPHERE/LOWER-STRATOSPHERE WATER VAPOR AND TRANSPORT INOT THE STRATOSPHERE" We propose to study the roles of the Asian and North American monsoons in transporting water vapor from the troposphere into the stratosphere. Extensive use of water vapor observations from the Aura platform will be used. Comparisons of the observations with both regional and global model analyses will serve to evaluate the quality of the data. The Aura platform will provide the highest resolution water vapor data yet available, so comparisons with mesoscale analyses are valuable in validating the data with non-coincidental measurements even though the mesoscale model is limited in spatial domain. Conditional probability distribution functions (PDF) will be the initial tool used to compare the satellite data with model analyses over a range of conditions including geographical location and atmospheric state. The PDF analysis will also include water vapor data from two instruments on the Aqua platform. This will permit inter-comparisons between the five instruments that measure upper-troposphere/lower-stratosphere water vapor on the Aura and Aqua platforms. The multi-scale investigation of monsoon-related transport into the stratosphere is unique in the use of a new global adjoint model and regional mesoscale models. The system shall be designed, fabricated, assembled and tested. As a minimum the URD and AA/LFT actuation system shall include: motors, planetary gear reduction and idler gear, Commutation and control feedback devices as required. Packaging into line replaceable unit(s) (LRU) shall be determined in the design cycle and finalized by the PDR. The design shall consider ease of maintenance, inspection and replacement of equipment and software as follows: (1) Adequate access for the inspection, service, maintenance, and replacement of LRUs. (2) Fully interchangeable components. (3) The design shall require no scheduled overhaul of components and minimal scheduled maintenance or service to maintain operation within the specified performance requirements. (4) The design shall provide for on-aircraft isolation of component failures and verification of system and component faults using either aircraft or external power. (5) The design shall allow on-aircraft maintenance to be performed using common tools and/or support equipment consistent with the support resources available at those airports compatible with the operation of the aircraft. (6) Any special tools required for installation or removal shall be fully detailed in the design. (7) The design shall contain features that eliminate the possibility of incorrect installation, or the inadvertent crossing of connections. (8) The software shall be of a modular design and all components of the development and verification environment identified. Description: THE MIXED-MORPHOLOGY SNR G359.1-0.5:  BIRTHPLACE OF THE MOUSE? We propose a 40 ksec XMM observation of the supernova remnant G359.1-0.5.  We will measure the column density towards G359.1-0.5, and thus determine whether this remnant may be located at the same distance as, and be associated with, the pulsar known as the Mouse. We will also study the morphology and spectral variations of this mixed-morphology remnant. Mixed-morphology, or thermal composite, remnants show a center-filled morphology that cannot be understood in the standard picture of supernova evolution. We aim to constrain the mechanisms of X-ray production from the center of this remnant, identifying whether thermal conduction, cloudlet evaporation, metallicity gradients, or other effects are primarily responsible for the observed center-filled morphology.

Description: STTR 2005, PHASE II PROJECT ENTITLED AERODYNAMIC EFFICIENCY ENHANCEMENTS FOR AIR VEHICLES. A system for autonomous detection and exploitation of weather phenomena for endurance or range enhancement for loitering unmanned air vehicles. The system is to consist of hardware and software for coarse identification of geographical areas where advantageous weather phenomena (such as soaring conditions) are present. Custom autopilot and sensors will enable the fine detection of the phenomena and cause the UAV to adopt an optimal flight path that exploits the phenomena. The system will consist of custom hardware, software, and sensors. A simulation of the system was demonstrated in Phase I, which is to be rendered in hardware in Phase II, including complete full flight test of the system on a 40 pound class UAV. The anticipated result being high endurance schemes for loitering UAVs, innovative flight control systems for UAVs, optimal flight path determination and execution. These developments dovetail with current NASA efforts to develop more intelligent and autonomous air vehicles for use in science mission, military and homeland security missions. The concepts and systems can be ported to small manned aircraft as well. The system as proposed can be used to increase the endurance or range, and/or reduce the fuel consumption of loitering air vehicles operating at low to medium altitudes. There are no UAVs currently having thermal soaring capability. By endowing UAVs with soaring capability, endurance can be enhanced and a framework will exist for next generation UAVs that can sense beneficial atmospheric conditions, couple it with data from online sources, and adapt to exploit the prevailing conditions optimally to achieve increased endurance range. These methods can be adopted for extending the endurance of small aircraft in emergency situations as well. The autopilot could be used by sport glider and motorglider pilots. Military, Homeland Security and science missions are increasing their uses of unmanned air vehicles. Use of this technology will also be investigated for small (<40 lb) and medium sized (~ 600 lb) UAVs which are being developed for homeland security and science missions.

C.1 STATEMENT OF WORKTHE CONTRACTOR S 2003-PHASE II PROPOSAL, NUMBER 03-II T6.01-9934, ENTITLED  PASSIVE WIRELESS MULTI-SENSOR TEMPERATURE AND PRESSURE SENSING SYSTEM USING ACOUSTIC WAVE DEVICES,  IS HEREBY INCORPORATED INTO THIS CONTRACT BY REFERENCE AS THE STATEMENT OF WORK.  THE FOLLOWING PAGES OF THE SAID PROPOSAL CONTAIN PROPRIETARY INFORMATION, AND SHALL THEREFORE NOT BE RELEASED OUTSIDE OF THE GOVERNMENT: ALL OF SECTION 3.2 WORK PLAN AND TABLE 5   PHASE II DELIVERABLES.DESCRIBES THE CONTINUED DEVELOPMENT OF PASSIVE, ORTHOGONAL FREQUENCY CODED (OFC) SURFACE ACOUSTIC WAVE (SAW) SENSORS AND MULTI-SENSOR SYSTEMS, AN ENABLING TECHNOLOGY FOR REMOTE WIRELESS SENSING OF TEMPERATURE,PRESSURE, AND A RANGE OF OTHER MEASURANDS, FOR APPLICATION TO SPACE EXPLORATIONS' DEMANDING ENVIROMENTS. PHASE I DEMONSTRATED THE TECHNICAL FEASIBILITY OF THE OFC APPROACH TO PRODUCE PASSIVE SOLID-STATE SAW SENSORS THAT CAN BE INTERROGATED REMOTELY USING RF SIGNALS, AND THAT RESPOND WITH A SIGNAL THAT ENCODES BOTH THE SENSOR'S IDENTITY AND TEMPERATURE MEASUREMENTS. OFC SAW TEMPERATURE SENSORS SIMILAR TO THOSE DEMONSTRATED IN PHASE I ARE CAPABLE OF OPERATING OVER TEMPERATURE RANGES NOT POSSIBLE WITH SILICON, FROM CRYOGENIC TO 1,000OC. THE SPREAD-SPECTRUM NATURE OF THE SYSTEM PROPOSED HEREIN, WHICH CONSISTS OF MULTIPLE PASSIVE OFC SAW SENSORS INTERROGATED REMOTELY USING CHIRPED RF SIGNALS, PROVIDES INCREASED PROCESSING GAIN AND GREATER COMMUNICATION SECURITY. THE PROPOSED PHASE II EFFORT WILL DEVELOP AND CHARACTERIZE PROTOTYPE OFC SAW TEMPERATURE SENSORS TARGETED TO SELECTED NASA AND COMMERCIAL APPLICATIONS, AND DEMONSTRATE PRESSURE SENSORS. THE TRANSCEIVER DESIGN WILL BE OPTIMIZED GIVEN THE SAW OPERATING PARAMETERS, CONVENTIONAL AND INNOVATIVE WAFER-LEVEL PACKAGING APPROACHES (FOR DEVICES CAPABLE OF WITHSTANDING EXTREME ENVIROMENTS) WILL BE DEVELOPED, AND A COMPLETE BREADBOARD WIRELESS MUTLI-SENSOR SYSTEM WILL BE DEMONSTRATED. THE SENSOR SYSTEM WILL PROVIDE A FLEXIBLE PLATFORM FOR REMOTE WIRELESS MONITORING OF A VARIETY OF POSSIBLE MEASURANDS. THE SMALL, LIGHTWEIGHT PASSIVE SENSORS, INITIALLY DESIGNED TO MEASURE TEMPERATURE AND PRESSURE, COULD POTENTIALLY BE APPLIED TO LIQUID VISCOSITY AND CHEMICAL SENSING APPLICATIONS.

Description: DAYTIME MULTIWAVEKLENGTH GROUND BASED OPTICAL INVESTIGATIONS OF PRECURSORS TO LOW LATITUDE PLASMA IRREGULARITIES ABSTRACT: We propose a 3-year systematic investigation of the precursors to the ESF irregularities during daytime using a ground-based multiwavelength Echelle spectrograph to be built at BU.  Equatorial Spread-F (ESF) refers to the presence of plasma irregularities at low- and equatorial latitudes in the nighttime ionosphere. ESF irregularities severely impact radio communications and navigational systems over a wide range of frequencies that adversely affect commercial and defense applications. The development of these irregularities is highly unpredictable. Even during the 'ESF season' when various onset parameters are nearly identical, ESF occurs on one night and is completely absent on the other. Scientifically, this is a key-missing element in our understanding of plasma instabilities at low latitudes. This proposed work will carry out daytime optical measurements to investigate the roles of neutral parameters, such as the meridional and vertical winds and waves that are known to be effective triggers to the ESF. For the first time in history, we will have a large field-of-view multiwavelength spectrograph that is ideally suited to answer these relevant issues. We will carry out simultaneous daytime measurements using three emissions at 5577, 6300 and 7774 A, which originate around 100, 230 and 300 km, respectively.  These measurements will enable us to investigate waves and their direction of propagation at three different altitudes. The results from this study will not only resolve issues surrounding the precursors to ESF but will also substantially enhance our understanding of the interaction of daytime and nighttime phenomena of the low-latitude/ equatorial electrodynamics in the upper atmosphere.  We plan to operate the new instrument at Carmen Alto, in Chile. This data will be used in conjunction with the multi-diagnostics of the Multi-Instrumented Studies of Equatorial Thermosphere Aeronomy (MISETA) consortium operating in the American longitude sector as well as Thermosphere Ionosphere Mesosphere Energetics and Dynamics (TIMED) satellite and Communicational/Navigational Outage Forecast System (C/NOFS) mission (scheduled to be launched in 2006). Furthermore, Jicamarca Unattended Long-term Investigations Atmosphere (JULIA) radar data, Jicamarca Radio Observatory (JRO) data, Global Positioning Systems (GPS) and Defense Meteorological Satellite Program (DMSP) data will be available for independent confirmation of the occurrence of ESF irregularities and for the information on the background thermosphere/ionosphere conditions in conjunction with our ground-based data. This dayglow data at multiple wavelengths will add to the rich database to the NASA LWS research and will be a unique resource to the aeronomy community.

Description: PROPOSAL TITLE: MULTI-INSTRUMENT INVESITGATION OF INNER-MAGNETOSPHERE/IONOSPHERE DISTURBANCES Strong penetrating and SAPS electric fields perturb and redistribute the cold plasma of the low and mid-latitude ionosphere and plasmasphere during geomagnetic disturbances. The phenomena associated with plasmasphere erosion are a prime example of global M-I coupling and require a multi-technique and multi-disciplinary analysis approach to understand properly. Streaming cold plasma, as seen as storm enhanced density SED plumes, can be used to identify and trace the effects of the perturbation electric fields. At lower latitudes, plasma redistribution and prompt changes in TEC indicate the effects of the disturbance electric fields. A thorough understanding of the mechanisms, causes and effects of these disturbance electric fields are needed to support a predictive capability for these important ionospheric phenomena. Questions to address: 1) Does the SAPS E field exhibit seasonal or longitude dependencies? 2) What determines the duration and strength of penetration electric field? 4) How do the conjugate E and F-region conductivities influence SAPS formation? 4) How does wave structure in the SAPS/SED channel lead to ionospheric irregularities? 5)What are the causes and characteristics of the redistribution of the equatorial ionosphere in the American sector? Proposed Method: 1)Use ionospheric TEC observations to study the location, extent, and duration of perturbation electric fields at mid and low latitudes. 2)Combine space and ground-based (GPS) TEC observations, incoherent-scatter radar (ISR) profiles, and DMSP observations to characterize the conditions leading to severe low-latitude ionospheric perturbation. 3) Investigate the relationship of the plasma redistribution to ionospheric irregularities using coherent radar, HF radio scintillation, and passive radar arrays (ISIS). 4)Coordinated ISR experiments (Sondrestrom, Millstone Hill, Arecibo, and Jicamarca) will investigate penetration E fields. 4) Modeling collaboration (RCM and SAMI-1I) to address the relationship of the observed features and their evolution to the predicted effects of ring current development and inner magnetospheric shielding. 6) Develop a multi-technique viewpoint of the coupled processes through workshops held at Haystack. 7) Coordinate a distributed working group to investigate storm phenomena using Access Grid and similar remote conferencing techniques. 8) TEC maps and merged datasets made available through the online Madrigal data system. This research program follows upon the considerable research that the PI institution has already undertaken on problems in this focused research area. The PI institution has organized a CEDAR working group on low-latitude electric field, and has designed and fielded instrumentation arrays (ISIS) to address electric-field structure, with continuous, spatially-distributed observations.

Description: MICROCLIMATE ZONES IN THE DRY VALLEYS OF ANTARCTICA:  IMPLICATIONS FOR LANDSCAPE EVOLUTION AND CLIMATE CHANGE ON MARS The Dry Valleys region of Antarctica is generally classified as a hyper-arid, cold-polar desert. The region has long been considered an important terrestrial analog for Mars because of its generally cold-and-dry climate and because it contains a suite of landforms at macro-, meso-, and microscales that resemble closely those observed on the Martian surface. On the basis of our recent recent work we propose to document these important Mars analog microenvironments for use by the Mars research and exploration community. The Dry Valleys region includes at least three microclimate zones and geomorphic processes and resultant landforms within these zones vary considerably. The microclimate zones include a coastal thaw zone, an inland mixed zone, and a stable upland frozen zone; zones are defined on the basis of varying atmospheric temperatures, soil moisture, and relative humidity. Subtle variations in these climate parameters result in considerable variation in the distribution and morphology of 1) gullies (macroscale features); 2) polygons, including ice-wedge, sand-wedge, and sublimation-type polygons, as well as viscous-flow features, including solifluction lobes, gelifluction lobes, and buried glaciers (mesoscale features); and 3) variations in rock-weathering processes/features, including salt weathering, thermals stress, wind erosion, and desert varnish (microscale features). One of the major goals of this proposal is to bring this important set of terrestrial cold-polar desert, microenvironment-Mars analogs to the Mars community in order to help quantify the atmospheric, climatological, and geologic processes on Mars and to make advances in our understanding of the evolution of climate, water, and potential habitats for extraterrestrial life. This study is thus designed to produce a geological dataset for important Mars-relevant environments on Earth that can be used in future research and automated and human exploration planning.

Description: Sources and Sinks of Carbon from Land-Use Change, Management, and Disturbance in the U.S.:  Steps Toward a Synthesis SOURCES AND SINKS OF CARBON FROM LAND-USE CHANGE, MANAGEMENT, AND DISTURBANCE IN THE U.S.: STEPS TOWARDS A SYNTHESIS ABSTRACT: A previous analysis by the principal investigator estimated the annual flux of carbon for the U.S. with census-based data on changes in land use, forestry, and fire management. The estimated sink in forests was low compared with studies based on data from forest inventories, but there were a number of processes omitted from the historical analysis. A reanalysis is warranted. The conterminous U.S. is a particularly good region for a detailed historical reconstruction because of the unusually rich assortment of historical data available. Landsat data on disturbance, available since 1972 offer a second data set, independent of census-based reconstructions of land-use change, for calculating sources and sinks of carbon during recent decades. These Landsat data are currently being compiled under on-going NACP projects. This proposal seeks support (1) to update the historical analysis based on census data and (2) to use the recent data compiled from the NACP Landsat analyses (3) to calculate two independent estimates of carbon flux for the conterminous U.S. over the period 1972-2000. Differences in the estimates of carbon flux (census-based versus Landsat-based) will reveal strengths and weakness of the two approaches and will be used to construct a harmonized estimate of carbon flux more accurate than possible from either approach by itself. For example, changes in land use obtained from the Landsat record miss disturbances before 1972 and thus underestimate both the area of recovering forests and the carbon accumulating in them. On the other hand, changes in land use based on census data (agricultural and forestry statistics) miss important processes affecting carbon storage (for example, natural disturbances). The overall objective of the proposed research is to determine the annual net flux of carbon for terrestrial ecosystems of the conterminous U.S. The emphasis will be on forests and will include the effects of forest conversion to agricultural land, abandonment of agricultural land, harvest of forests, other forms of forest management, wildfires, other disturbances, and forest growth. The approach will use an improved carbon model with two independent data sets of land-use/cover change: one, historical census data; the second, recent Landsat data. Model results will be tested against SRTM-derived estimates of aboveground biomass (from another on-going NACP project). The results of the proposed research are expected to contribute significantly to NASALS goals in at least two respects. First, the research will produce a new estimate of carbon flux for the conterminous U.S. The estimate will be spatially specific, based on a harmonization of historical, census data and Landsat data. The results will include an evaluation of the error of the estimated flux, including the effect of spatial resolution on error. Second, the research will produce a spatial/historical (1700-2005) data set of land-use change for the forests of the U.S.

Description: "SENSOR WEB DYNAMIC REPLANNING" We will propose to extend the dynamic replanning capability of Draper's Earth Phenomena Observing System (EPOS), which has successfully demonstrated the capability to dynamically replan the activities of NASA space-based sensor assets to maximize the return of useful science measurements (e.g., ensure cloud free targeting). We will propose to enhance and extend EPOS to include the replanning of sensors on UAVs (Unmanned Aerial Vehicles) and USVs (Unmanned Surface Vessels) being fielded by NASA over the next few years. The new dynamic replanning capability will utilize complementary and cooperative suites of heterogeneous sensor assets that can be triggered by observation data and/or predictive models to adaptively respond to significant events and provide enhanced understanding of temporal Earth phenomena. An event-driven use of a sensor web would be to task sensor resources in response to observation-triggered cues for phenomenon, such as harmful algal bloom outbreaks. A model-driven use of a sensor web would be to task sensor resources in response to significant increases in meteorological forecast model error growth due to model sensitivities within specific atmospheric regions. The events and phenomena that present the largest potential payoff to the proposed replanning capability are characterized by being localized and transient and also capable of causing damage to both human life and property, e.g., weather (tornadoes, hurricanes, etc.), harmful algal blooms, volcanic eruptions, ice shelf break-up, seismic activities, oil spilis, and search and rescue. In addition, the replanning capability will be enhanced to handle outages and failures of individual sensors.

Description: VOLVANIC PLUMES ON MARS AND VENUS This proposal comprises three tasks to continue ongoing research to study explosive volcanic eruption plumes on Mars and Venus. Over the last 30 years, there have been numerous models for explosive volcanic eruption columns based on the basic ideas for convecting plumes presented by Morton et al. #124;1956#124;. Our prior efforts [Glaze and Baloga, 2002), however, indicated that these accepted plume models are not valid for most plausible conditions on Mars, and that basic model assumptions were not strictly valid on Earth or Venus. Under current PGG funding, we have developed a new approach to buoyant plume modeling that addresses the fundamental assumptions of pressure balance [Glaze and Baloga, 2005). We propose to build on the success that we have had in developing this new plume model in an effort to revise thinking as regards explosive volcanic eruption column dynamics. The primary objectives of the three proposed tasks are to 1) develop a robust model, based on the new Glaze and Baloga [2005] approach, that Is fully time dependent describing plumes with gas, liquid and solid components, and with the ability for solids to be transported at a different velocity, 2) modify the basic model developed under Task 1 in order to explore the importance of linear vent sources (i.e., fissures and flood volcanism), and 3) incorporate new constraints on the boundary conditions for the central and linear vent models developed in Tasks 1 and 2 based on recent terrestrial experience.

Description: JOHNS HOPKINS UNIVERSITY HI, DI AND OTHER ABUNDANCES ALONG THREE EXTENDED SIGHTLINES Measurements of the DIH and DIO ratios have been shown to be remarkably constant up to logN(H) -19.2, which corresponds roughly to the limits of the Local Bubble. Between 19.2 < 10gN(H) < 20.6, these ratios present a large scatter, while for logN(H) > 20.6 DIH and DIO seem to be constant again. albeit with values roughly half that of the Local Bubble. Although several mechanisms have been proposed to explain these variations, a global consistent picture of these abundance patterns is still missing. The low yield of high column density sightlines suitable for accurate DIH measurements has bun a major barrier to progress in this area. This derives from the extreme difficulty of finding suitable targets at these high column densities, both in terms of DI not being obscured by either HI or H2 absorption and having data available to determine reliable HI column densities from Lya. This proposal requests additional observing time to obtain signal-to-noise ratios adequate for determining the column densities of DI, NI, 01, and Fell, along three high N(H) sightlines that have been previously observed by FUSE. Preliminary analyses of the current datasets show that these sightlines are suitable for DI measurements. Existing high resolution HST/STIS data for the three sightlines will be used to determine N(Hl) along two of the sightlines (N(Hl) has been published for the other one) as well as to model the velocity structure along the sightlines.  These datasets will also allow us to determine the abundances of species that do not have unsaturated transitions in the FUSE bandpass (SI, Ni11, etc.). Additionally, N(OI) derived from the weaker, but with a more reliable f-value. 1356A transition in the STIS bandpass will be compared to the one derived from the 974 A transition in the FUSE bandpass.

Description: THE VALIDATION OF AURA OZONE MEASUREMENTS USING CLOUD SLICING This proposal is in response to NASA Research Announcement (Earth Science Enterprise NNH04ZYS004N) titled "Measurements, Modeling and Analysis in Support of Aura and other NASA Satellite Observations of the Earth's Atmosphere". The main objective of our proposal is to construct a data base for stratospheric and tropospheric column ozone using EP TOMS version 8 data overlapping with Aura. These data will be used for validation of ozone measurements from OMI, HIRDLS, MLS, and TES instruments on the Aura satellite. The methodology used for deriving stratospheric and tropospheric column ozone is based on Cloud Slicing using deep convective clouds in the Pacific region. This method gives an accurate measurement of stratospheric and tropospheric column amount from the tropics tc middle-and-high-latitudes as has been shown by comparing-with-20-years of stratospheric ozone measurements from SAGE (version 6.2) and many years of tropospheric ozone measurements from ozonesondes obtained from WOUDC and SHADOZ programs. A second objective of this proposal is to construct a nearly continuous data base of tropospheric and stratospheric column ozone from 1979 to the present time by combining Nimbus-7, EP TOMS, and Aura measurements to address several key questions ranging from the effects of regional pollution to the recovery of stratospheric ozone. The effects of regional and global pollution will be studied using global models of tropospheric chemistry and transport such as MOZART-2.

Description: Understanding the Evolution and Impacts of Storm-Enhanced Electric Fields in the Mid-Latitude Ionosphere The proposal is directed to the NASA LWS TR&T Targeted Invesigation program element and addresses the Focused Science Topic, 'Storm effects on the global electrodynamics and the middle and low latitude ionosphere, which is identified by program descriptor T3d. We seek a deeper understanding of the penetration of nominally high-latitude ionospheric electric fields into the mid and low-latitude ionosphere and accordingly into the inner magnetosphere. Electric fields and plasma convection are of high importance for both scientific understanding and operations; in the inner magnetosphere they contribute to the circulation of energetic particles, the energization of plasma, the creation of plasma pressure gradients and the generation of fieldaligned currents; in the ionosphere they redistribute plasma, generate ionospheric structure, and populate the medium with irregularities through processes of plasma instability. During quiet periods the electric field is largely confined to the high-latitude zone and is highly variable in both time and space. During geomagnetic storms the electric field penetrates into the inner magnetosphere where it produces significant changes in magnetosphere-ionosphere coupling and major changes in the subauroral ionosphere. The ionospheric effects adversely impact modern technological systems including communications, surveillance, and global positioning. Two of the major goals of LWS science are to understand the processes that lead to these disturbances and to predict when they will occur. Reaching these goals requires a significantly improved understanding of the spatial and temporal evolution of both ionospheric and magnetospheric electric fields during storms.

Description: Land Information Sensor Web This project will develop a prototype Land Information Sensor Web by integrating the Land Information System (LIS) in a sensor web framework will allow for optimal 2-way information flow that enhances land surface modeling using sensor web observations, and in turn allows sensor web reconfiguration to minimize overall system uncertainty. Through continuous automatic calibration techniques and data assimilation methods, LIS will enable on-the-fly sensor web reconfiguration to optimize the changing needs of science and solutions. This prototype will be based on a simulated interactive sensor web, which is then used to exercise and optimize the sensor web modeling interfaces. These synthetic experiments provide a controlled environment in which to examine the end-to-end performance of the prototype, and examine the impact of various design sensor web design trade-offs and the eventual value of sensor webs for particular prediction or decision support. In addition to providing critical Information for sensor web design considerations, this prototype would establish legacy for operational sensor web integration with modeling systems. Though the stand-alone LIS has achieved a TRL of 8, we determine our entry TRL to be 4 as other components are to be implemented and tested. This project will deliver an interoperable TRL 6 plug-and-play components based on LIS that enable data ingest and scientific analysis, the generation of new sensor web data products, connections to major spacecraft schedulers and task managers, metadata transformation and exchange, and data fusion techniques. This project directly addresses topic area 3: Enabling model interactions with sensor webs, and is expected to have a 3-year performance period starting from October 2006.

Description: Land Information Sensor Web This project will develop a prototype Land Information Sensor Web by integrating the Land Information System (LIS) in a sensor web framework will allow for optimal 2-way information flow that enhances land surface modeling using sensor web observations, and in turn allows sensor web reconfiguration to minimize overall system uncertainty. Through continuous automatic calibration techniques and data assimilation methods, LIS will enable on-the-fly sensor web reconfiguration to optimize the changing needs of science and solutions. This prototype will be based on a simulated interactive sensor web, which is then used to exercise and optimize the sensor web modeling interfaces. These synthetic experiments provide a controlled environment in which to examine the end-to-end performance of the prototype, and examine the impact of various design sensor web design trade-offs and the eventual value of sensor webs for particular prediction or decision support. In addition to providing critical Information for sensor web design considerations, this prototype would establish legacy for operational sensor web integration with modeling systems. Though the stand-alone LIS has achieved a TRL of 8, we determine our entry TRL to be 4 as other components are to be implemented and tested. This project will deliver an interoperable TRL 6 plug-and-play components based on LIS that enable data ingest and scientific analysis, the generation of new sensor web data products, connections to major spacecraft schedulers and task managers, metadata transformation and exchange, and data fusion techniques. This project directly addresses topic area 3: Enabling model interactions with sensor webs, and is expected to have a 3-year performance period starting from October 2006.

Description: The self-adaptive Earth Predictive System (SEPS) concept combines Earth System Models (ESM) and Earth Observations (EO) into one system. EO measures the Earth system state while ESM predicts the evolution of the state. A feedback mechanism processes EO measurements and feeds them into ESM during model runs or as initial conditions. A feed-forward mechanism analyzes the ESM predictions against science goals for scheduling optimized/targeted observations. The SEPS framework automates the Feedback and Feed-forward mechanisms (theFF-loop). Scientists from GMU, GSFC, and UBMC will collaborate to 1) develop a general SEPS framework for dynamic, interoperable coupling between ESMs and EO, based on open, consensus-based standards; 2) inplement and deploy the the framework and plug in diverse sensors and data systems to demonstrate the plug-in-EO-and-play capability; and 3) prototype a Bird- Migration-Model-to-aid-avian-influenza-prediction SEPS and an atmospheric chemistry composition SEPS using this framework, to demonstrate the frameworks' plug-in-ESM-and-play capability and its applicability as a common infrastructure for supporting the focus areas of NASA research. This project will significantly advance 1) dynamic, interoperable and live coupling of ESM with the sensor web; 2) the sensor web from concept to peration with existing sensors and data sources; and 3) the use of service-oriented architecture in modeling and integration. The project will improve the accuracy and timeliness of monitoring and predicting rapidly changing Earch phenomena, suca as sever weather and air pollution. The 3-year project will start in October 2006. The entry TRL is 4 ad the exit TRL is 7.

Description: "REMOTE MONITORING OF CHANGES IN FOREST FUNCTIONAL TYPES AFTER DISTURBANCE FROM FIRE IN THE NORTH AMERICAN BOREAL REGION: IMPLICATIONS FOR INTERPRETING THE EFFECTS OF SATELLITE-OBSERVED CHANGES IN" A three year research proposal is presented with a goal to both map and gain a better understanding of the factors controlling transitions between black spruce and deciduous forestslparklandslgrasslands that occur at deeadal scales during succession after fires in the North American boreal region (NABR). Black spruce forests function as a major terrestrial carbon reservoir in the NABR, represent 50% of the forest cover in this region, and can be thought of as a distinctly different forest functional type than the deciduous forests found in this region because they contain deep organic layers. In particular, our study will focus on the linkage between fire, climate and changes in post-fire successional processes that lead to converting spruce forests to deciduous forests. Our research will focus on addressing the following hypothesis: transitions from black spruce to alternative forestJnon-forest functional types are controlled by variations in (a) post-fire organic-layer depth (surface burn severity), (b) soil moisture (affected by precipitation and site drainage); (e) soil temperature (affected by organic layer depth, elevation, and aspect); and (d) seed-source availability (distance to nearest deciduous tree seed source i dispersal distance). The research will be carried out by an interdisciplinary research team from the Universities of Maryland and Alaska and General Dynamics, with all the members having extensive significant research experience in the NABR. In this study, we will use MODIS and Landsat TMiETM imagery to analyze and map different trajectories of post-fire succession in forest stands in AlaskaNukon Territories in areas that burned between 1970 and 1999. We will use Landsat TM imagery to map pre-fire forest cover and to estimate burn severity. We will use imaging radar data from ERS, ENVISAT, and Radarsat to estimate variations in post-fire soil moisture. Field studies will be used collect data to validate the remotely sensed data and collect additional observations on site characteristics where different patterns of post-fire succession occurs. Finally, using the data collected during this study, as well as field data collected by a CO-I under a Joint Fire Science Project and by Collaborators at sites being studied by the National Park Service and through the Bonanza Creek LTER, we will develop a conceptual model to link the satellite observations to the processes which are controlling post-fire succession. The results from this study will provide a clearer understanding of how satellite imagery can be used to study patterns of post-fire succession and carbon cycling in the NABR region. These results will enable scientists involved in the North American Carbon Cycle Science program to more clearly interpret the changes in vegetation greenness that have been observed in the NABR through examination of the longer term satellite record based on AVHRR imagery. Finally, the results from this study will be important in improving models of terrestrial carbon cycling because they will provide an improved understanding of the factors that lead to transitions between two important forest functional types found in the NABR.

Description: Probing the Central Regions of Nearby Galaxies Observed by Galex and Spitzer Legacy Projects NASA's Galaxy Evolution Explorer (GALEX) is conducting wide-field imaging and spectroscopic surveys in FUV (1350-1750A) and NUV (1750-3000A) bands. A dedicated campaign to image 300+ nearby galaxies (Nearby Galaxy Survey, NGS) is nearly complete. We propose FUSE survey observations for the central region of 25 galaxies with completed GALEX imaging, which are also being observed at 3.6-160^m as part of either the Spitzer Infrared Nearby Galaxy Survey (SINGS) or Mid-IR Hubble Atlas (MIR-atlas) projects. Our sample galaxies span a wide range of star formation activity in the local universe. The FUSE spectra, when combined with GALEX and Spitzer observations, will constrain the star formation history (SFH) in the central region of each target, placing the sample into an evolutionary context. The SFH will be estimated via direct comparison with reddened Starburst99 population synthesis predictions, improved by the FUSE spectral library of hot stars. Our analysis will be based on the FUV to UV continuum slope, spectral line diagnostics, and the overall FUV-FIR SED. We will concurrently determine the FUV attenuation law with unprecedented accuracy for ordinary star-forming galaxies, and test for correlation of the extinction law with SFH and galaxy type, given that copious star formation may modify dust grain properties. The combination of FUSE, GALEX, and Spitzer data provides a rare opportunity to decisively test and calibrate the IRX-/3 attenuation-reddening relation, which may be used to gauge UV extinction for > 107 galaxies detected in the GALEX imaging surveys. Our GALEX FUV, NUV imagery was used to select targets and will aid interpretation of spatially integrated FUSE spectra. Radial profiles and spatially-resolved SEDs in UV-IR bands will allow us to extend our results beyond the circumnuclear region. The proposed dataset will have additional archival value, given the GALEX/SINGS Legacy program

Description: GLOBAL ENERGY AND WATER CYCLE EXPERIMENT (GEWEX), INTERNATIONAL PROJECT OFFICE (GPO) GEWEX has set the stage for broader issues to be addressed within the water cycle initiatives of NASA, as well as the US Global Change Research Program, IGOS-P, the joint International GeosphereBiospshere Program (IGBP), and the International Human Dimensions Programme (IHDP), GEWEX is essentially an implementing arm of these broader science water cycle initiatives and the Phase II efforts are pilot projects where the applicable activities can be used, modified, or transitioned to meet the broader NASA Water Cycle goals. Clearly, the supporting GEWEX science community and the agency programs, such as the Earth Science Program, provide the resources, guidance, involvement, and impetus without which none of the activities could proceed; however, the IGPO is necessary to provide the implementing continuity to address the longer-term issues, larger-scale activities, and multiagency/ international cooperation. During GEWEX Phase II, IGPO will place priority on satisfying the following objectives: Producing consistent research quality data sets complete with error descriptions of the Earth's energy budget and water cycle and their variability and trends on interannual to decadal time scales, and for use in climate system analysis and model development and validation. Enhancing the understanding of how energy and water cycle processes function and quantify their contribution to climate feedbacks. Determining the geographical and seasonal characteristics of the predictability of key water and energy cycle variables over land areas and through collaborations with the wider WCRP community determine the predictability of energy and water cycles on a global basis. Developing better seasonal predictions of water and energy cycle variability through improved parameterizations encapsulating hydrometeorological processes and feedbacks for atmospheric circulation models. Undertaking joint activities with operational ydrometeorological services and hydrological research programs to demonstrate the value of new GEWEX prediction capabilities, data sets and tools for assessing the consequences of global change.

Description: THE MOST LUMINOUS TYPE 2 QSO IN SDSS EXPLORATION OF THE HELIOSPHERE BY SOLAR BACKSCATTERED LYMAN ALPHA RADIATION: INTERPRETATION OF VOYAGER AND PIONEER LYMAN ALPHA MEASUREMENTS The primary purpose of this program is to enhance our knowledge of the heliosphere through the study of the backscattered Lyman Alpha glow. The key, central objectives of this project are to study the time-dependence of the heliosphere, to estimate the very local interstellar medium (VLISM) neutral hydrogen density and to investigate the effect of the squeezing of the heliospheric interface by the interstellar magnetic field on the observed Lyman Alpha glow which would require the use of 3-d modeling of the heliosphere. The objectives will be attained using time-dependent heliospheric models with and without interstellar magnetic fields to calculate backscattered Lyman Alpha glow and compare with the post-1998 Voyager 1 Lyman Alpha data and also with the Lyman Alpha glow observed by Voyager 2 and Pioneer 10 ultraviolet detectors at different heliocentric distances and times. This project is made possible by the existence of the interplanetary Lyman Alpha background data collected by deep space spacecraft Pioneer 10/11 (P10/11) and Voyager 1/2 (V1/2) during their more than 25 years of exploration of the heliosphere. The proposed work will greatly improve our understanding of the time-dependence of the heliosphere and check the eliability of a current state of the art heliosphere models. Recently proposed time-dependent heliospheric models are the only detailed pictures of the sun-galaxy interaction available at present. The proposed work will test the accuracy of our current knowledge of the sun-galaxy interaction and is thus highly relevant to Nasa's Sun-Earth connection quest about the Sun-Galaxy interaction. The proposed work neatly fits in with a major quest posed by the Sun-Earth onnection Roadmap," How do the Sun and Galaxy interact?". The relevance of our proposed work is clearly demonstrated from the following quote from the Roadmap, "of special interest is the nature of the interface between the solar wind and the interstellar medium and the physical processes that occur there". This clearly shows that the proposed research is directly related to the NASA Sun-Earth connection Roadmap, Pioneer and Voyager interstellar programs through optimization of the future "Interstellar Probe" mission and its instrumentation. Our models and results can also be applied to the interpretation of Cassini measurements of Lyman Alpha background made during its cruise to Saturn.

Description: A STUDY OF COMETARY ACTIVITY USING MEASUREMENTS BY  THE SOLAR WIND ANISOTROPIES (SWAN) INSTRUMENT ON SOHO Atomic hydrogen is the most abundant species in the atmopshere (or coma) of a comet.  Most hydogren is produced in a photodissociation chain originating with water, and water is the most abundant volatile species in a comet's nucleus.  Measurement of the abundance and distribution of hydrogen in the coma, when appopriately modeled, can provide a reliable time history measure of the water production rate in comets.  Virtually all compositional information is compared to water, making water the most important for obtainning accurate production rates.  Variations in production rates with time generally, and with heliocentric distance in particular, provide information about the composition and structure of the nucleus.  Determining the activity of Oort cloud comets, which are likely composed of the most pristine material in the solar system, and Jupiter Family Comets which are pieces of Kuiper Belt Objects and the targets of past and upcoming missions to comets are both critical for both similar and highly complementary reasons.  the objectives of this program address the analysis of observations of the LYman-alpha comae of a number of comets that have been observed by the Swan instrument on the SOHO spacecraft.  We have developed significant model analysis tools for extracting detailed daily-averages of water production rates from sequences of images of the H Lyman-alpha coma.  While the SWAN instrument continues to operate and observe new comets, a considerable archive of observations of over 50 comets already exists since the first observatrions of comet Hyakutake in 1996.  Our specific science goals are (1) to analyze a statistically significant sample of comets, of various taxnomic types and and over as wide range of heliocentric distance as possible, (2) to study their production rate variations with time, covering both long time scales (heliocentric distance dependence) as well as short times scales to investigate outbursts, fragmentation and splitting which can provide valuable information about cometary nuclei, (3) to perform a particular study of Deep Space 1 target comet 19P/Borrelly, and (4) to study the variation of hydrogen lifetime and water photochemistry over solar cycle.

Description: INTEGRATING REMOTELY-SENSED IMAGERY AND SOCIAL SURVEYS FOR SUSTAINABILITY:  THE CASE OF US/MEXICO BORDERLANDS (GRADUATE STUDENT:  NEIL CARTER) The overall goals ofthis project were to understand and predict how socio-political processes affect the environment in the Lower Rio Grand Valley (LRGV; Fig. 1). The project has 5 specific and interrelated objectives: 1) evaluate how NAFTA impacted sustainability (e.g., primary productivity and land cover), 2) identify publicly perceived threats to environmental sustainability, 3) determine attributes of individuals who have constraints (e.g., low education, low income) against participation in environmental decision making (e.g., land use planning) but still participate, 4) compare environmental world views of groups living in degraded environments and healthier environments, and 5) model and simulate spatio-temporal dynamics of human-environment relationships under different policy scenarios. To achieve the objectives, I will use remote sensing, household surveys, field notes, data from previous and ongoing studies, census data, and systems modeling and simulation. Spatially explicit data collected through remote sensing (Normalized Difference Vegetation Index data and Landsat TM images) will provide linkages between policy, human population, and land cover change in the systems model. Further, remotely sensed data will allow evaluation of land use and primary productivity change in Mexican areas of the border region where fine scale (below state) social data is not available. I will use a systems approach to integrate all components, and use a landscape perspective to evaluate spatial patterns and human-environment interactions. The results will begin to explicate the linkages between social and environmental systems in trans-boundary contexts. As the first attempt to evaluate NAFTAs impact on land cover and primary productivity in the U.S.-Mexico borderlands, this proposed project will have significant implications for coupled human-environment systems theory, method, and application. The systems model will facilitate scaling up from this study area to other trans-boundary contexts (e.g., the 1-69 corridor).

Description: EFFECTS OF RHEOLOGY ON THE DYNAMICS AND EVOLUTION OF PLANETARY INTERIORS The objective of this proposal is to understand the nature of the fundamental differences between the planets using observational data as well as improved physical models of mantle processes. Our studies have shown that the rheology of rocks has a major effect on mantle dynamics and evolution. In particular, we found that it is highly unlikely for plate tectonics to begin after a planet has completely crystallized. On small planets, such as Mars and Mercury, not only plate tectonics but any type of mantle convection seems to be problematic. In the past we could only study mantle dynamics with realistic rheologies in two dimensions. With the rapid growth of computing power it has become possible to systematically investigate mantle dynamics in fully three-dimensional spherical shell geometry. The realistic rheology of rocks and three dimensional geometry are two computationally challenging factors. Putting them together will be a major step forward. We will be able to model the whole planet over its entire evolution as opposed to regional modeling in a narrow time window. This will allow us to use a substantially larger set of observational data to constrain planetary evolution. This will help us to better understand the mechanisms of global resurfacing of Venus around 750 million years ago and the formation of different types of upwellings on this planet. We will explore the origin of different global patterns of mantle convection on the terrestrial planets such as a long-lived single plume in the Martian mantle versus multi-plume structure on Venus. We will also develop new models of crystallization of the Mercurian core, which are based on new experimental constraints on the phase diagram of iron and which can help to explain the small change in planetary radius during secular cooling of this planet. In addition, we will continue the fluid dynamical investigation of convection-induced stresses to understand the observed patterns of crustal deformation on planetary bodies and will address the question of applicability of the sluggish lid regime of temperature-dependent viscosity convection to the dynamics of planetary interiors. Our three-dimensional modeling will be guided and complemented by theoretical analysis, parameterized convection calculations and two-dimensional models.

Description: "ELEVATION CHANGE, MASS BALANCE, AND SEA LEVEL CONTRIBUTION FROM THE GREENLAND ICE SHEET AND COASTAL OUTLET GLACIERS USING ICESAT AND CRYOSAT DATA" THE FOCUS OF OUR PROPOSED RESEARCH WILL BE TO MEASURE ELEVATION CHANGE, MASS BALANCE, AND SEA-LEVEL CONTRIBUTIONS FROM THE GREENLAND ICE SHEET AND ITS COASTAL OUTLET GLACIERS BY EXPLOITING BOTH ICESAT AND CRYOSAT DATA.  ICESAT AND CRYOSAT DATA WILL PROVIDE IMPORTANT NEW OBSERVATIONS OF GREENLAND S COASTAL AREAS WHICH ARE UNDERGOING RAPID CHANGE. MOREOVER, WE PROPOSE TO LINK THE ICESAT AND CRYOSAT ELEVATION TIME SERIES TO THE DECADAL+ TIME SERIES PROVIDED BY ERS-1, ERS-2, AND ENVISAT SATELLITES TO PROVIDE IMPORTANT CONTEXT THAT WILL SIGNIFICANTLY ENHANCE THE UTILITY AND INTERPRETATION OF BOTH THE ICESAT AND CRYOSAT RESULTS.  MAJOR OBJECTIVES OF THIS RESEARCH ARE:  1) TO CONSTRUCT RECENT ELEVATION-CHANGE TIME SERIES FOR ALL OF GREENLAND S MAJOR COASTAL OUTLET GLACIERS USING BOTH ICESAT AND CRYOSAT DATA. CROSS CALIBRATION OF ICESAT AND CRYOSAT DATA, ASSUMING TIME OVERLAP, COULD PROVIDE SIGNIFICANT BENEFIT TO BOTH SATELLITE DATASETS.  2) TO CONSTRUCT RECENT ICESAT AND CRYOSAT ELEVATION-CHANGE TIME SERIES FOR THE GREENLAND ICE SHEET INTERIOR AND LINK THESE TO ERS-1/ERS-2/ENVISAT TIME SERIES TO PLACE THESE MEASUREMENTS IN LONG-TERM CONTEXT. 3) TO COMPARE AND ANALYZE LONG-TERM ELEVATION-CHANGE TIME SERIES WITH EXTENSIVE ICE CORE DATA IN SOUTHERN GREENLAND TO UNDERSTAND THE INFLUENCE OF ACCUMULATION HISTORY AND VARIABILITY.  IN PARTICULAR, THIS WILL IMPROVE UNDERSTANDING OF THE MULTI-DECADE THINNING IN SOUTHEAST GREENLAND WHICH MAY BE DUE TO THE MIGRATION OF THE DYNAMIC THINNING OF THE COASTAL OUTLET GLACIERS TO THE INLAND CATCHMENT AREAS OF THE UPPER ELEVATIONS. 4) TO PRODUCE RECENT AND LONG-TERM ESTIMATES OF THE GREENLAND ICE SHEET S CONTRIBUTION TO GLOBAL SEA LEVEL RISE.  RECENT ESTIMATES WILL INCLUDE COASTAL AND INTERIOR ICE-SHEET COMPONENTS, WHILE LONG-TERM ESTIMATES WILL BE BASED ON INTERIOR ICE-SHEET MEASUREMENTS ONLY. THE PROPOSED RESEARCH IS RELEVANT TO NASA S NATIONAL OBJECTIVE FOR THE DEVELOPMENT AND USE OF ADVANCED EARTH OBSERVATION CAPABILITIES FROM SPACE. GOTH ICESAT AND CRYOSAT REPRESENT SIGNIFICANT ADVANCEMENTS IN ALTIMETRIC OBSERVATION OF THE EARTH FROM SPACE. MOREOVER, THIS RESEARCH SPECIFICALLY ADDRESSES KEY SCIENTIFIC OBJECTIVES OF NASA S CLIMATE VARIABILITY AND CHANGE (CVC) ROADMAP BY: 1) MEASURING RECENT AND LONG-TERM CHANGES IN GREENLAND ICE TOPOGRAPHY AND MASS BALANCE. 2) ESTIMATING THE RECENT (COASTAL AND INTERIOR) AND LONG-TERM (INTERIOR) CONTRIBUTIONS OF THE GREENLAND ICE SHEET TO SEA-LEVEL RISE. 3) PERFORMING ANALYSES TO UNDERSTAND AND/OR INTERPRET THE RESULTS IN TERMS OF NATURAL VARIABILITY OR DYNAMIC CHANGE.

Description: RADIOISOTOPE POWER CONVERSION TECHNOLOGY.  THIS PROGRAM ADDRESSES THE REQUEST FOR RPS CONVERSION TECHNOLOGY DEVELOPMENT IN NRA-02-OSS-01.  THE GOAL OF THE PROJECT IS TO DEMONSTRATE A STATIC TPV POWER CONVERTER SUITABLE FOR USE WITH AN ADVANCED RPS USING GPHS HEAT SOURCES, BRINGING THIS CONVERTER TECHNOLOGY (RTPV) TO TRL 5 AT THE END OF THE THIRD YEAR.  TPV CONVERTS RADIANT ENERGY FROM A HOT EMITTER TO ELECTRICAL POWER USING PV CELLS.  TPV USES ADVANCED PV CELLS TO UTILIZE A BROADER, SPECTRALLY-TUNED RANGE OF WAVELENGTHS FOR MORE EFFICIENT POWER CONVERSION THAN SOLAR PV CELLS.  SPECTRAL CONTROL, INCLUDING SELECTIVE EMITTER, PV CELL, AND FILTER CHARACTERISTICS, IS KEY TO HIGH PERFORMANCE.  LIFETIME TESTS ARE PLANNED.  STEPS IN THE DEVELOPMENT INCLUDE: YEAR 1:  DEVELOP THE TPV MODULE (TRL 3) - DEVELOP, FABRICATE, DEMONSTRATE AND SELECT THE BEST OPTIONS FROM VARIOUS EMITTERS, PV CELLS, AND FILTER APPROACHES, WITH SUPPORT EFFORTS TO DEVELOP THE PRELIMINARY CONVERTER DESIGN AND TO ADDRESS TWO KEY TECHNICAL QUESTIONS ABOUT CONVERTER LIFETIME:  RADIATION EFFECTS ON THE PV CELLS AND MATERIALS TRANSFER.  YEAR 2:  DEMONSTRATE A PROTOTYPIC RTPV OPTICAL CAVITY/CONVERTER (TRL 4) - FABRICATE AND TEST AN ELECTRICALLY HEATED BASELINE CONVERTER WITH PROTOTYPICAL DESIGN (OPTICAL CAVITY/CONVERTER AND IMMEDIATE STRUCTURE), WITH SUPPORTING MODELING AND TESTING EFFORTS, AS WELL AS CONTINUE RADIATION EXPOSURE AND MATERIALS LIFE TESTS.  YEAR 3:  DEMONSTRATE A BREADBOARD RTPV OPTICAL CAVITY/CONVERTER AND LONG-TERM PERFORMANCE OF A PROTOTYPIC CONVERTER (TRL 5) - BUILD A BREADBOARD MODEL WITH THE OPTIMUM CONVERTER DESIGN AND A POWER CONVERTER MODULE, THEN TEST IN A THERMAL VACUUM CHAMBER; CONCLUDE SUPPORTING EFFORTS TO DEMONSTRATE LONG LIFE WITH MINIMAL POWER DECREASE.  RECENT ADVANCES IN INGAAS PV CELL, FILTER, AND SLECTIVE EMITTER TECHNOLOGY HAVE SIGNIFICANTLY IMPROVED THE PERFORMANCE OF TPV SYSTEMS TO THE POINT THAT TPV SYSTEMS ARE NOW COMPETITIVE IN CONVERSION EFFICIENCY A ND SPECIFIC POWER WITH DYNAMIC POWER SYSTEMS.  SPECIFICALLY, TPV CONVERTER EFFIFIENCY OF 20% HAS BEEN DEMONSTRATED AT 1330 K FOR SINGLE CELLS (SIERGIEJ ET AL. 2002) AND FOR A 16-CELL ARRAY IN AN OPTICAL CAVITY DURING THE YEAR 1 EFFORT.  WE EXPECT TO IMPROVE ON THIS.

IT HAS BEEN PREDICTED THAT THESE TWO STATES WILL HAVE LONG RELAXATION AND COHERENCE TIMES.  THE TWO ELECTRON STATES HAVE DIFFERENT AMPLITUDES AT THE DONOR NUCLEUS AND THUS THE HYPERFINE INTERACTION WITH THE NUCLEAR SPIN IS  DIFFERENT.  HERE IT IS PROPOSED TO USE PULSED ELECTRON SPIN RESONANCE (ESR) TO TIME RESOLVE THE EVOLUTION OF THE HYPERFINE LINES AND THUS PROBE THE RELAXATION PROCESSES.  TECHNIQUES WILL BE DEVELOPED TO APPLY UNIAXIAL STRESS TO THE SI IN THE PULSED-ESR CAVITY AT TEMPERATURE DOWN TO 300MK.      A PARTICULARLY INTERESTING ASPECT OF THE DONOR STATES FOR SI:LI IS THE COUPLING BETWEEN THEM AND THE SPIN OF THE ELECTRON BOUND TO THE DONOR.  IN THE GROUND STATE (WHEN STRESS IS APPLIED) THERE IS NO HYPERFINE INTERACTION BETWEEN THE ELECTRON AND THE SPIN OF THE LI NUCLEUS SINCE THE VALLEY STATE IS ANTISYMMETRIC.  HOWEVER, IN THE EXCITED STATE (WITH STRESS) THE VALLEY COMBINATION IS NOT ANTISYMMETRIC, AND THERE IS A NON-ZERO HYPERFINE INTERACTION, AS SEEN BY WATKINS AND HAM, [5] IN CW-ESR EXPERIMENTS. ABOVE-GAP EXCITATION LEADS TO THE FORMATION OF BOUND EXCITONS AT THESE TEMPERATURES, WHICH DECAY THROUGH AN AUGER PROCESS.  THE RECAPTURE OF THE ELECTRONS PRODUCES COMPARABLE POPULATIONS OF THE 1>AND 0>STATES, WITH THE 1>THEN DECAYING WITH A TIME.  T, TO THE GROUND STATE.  THIS DECAY CAN BE MONITORED WITH A PULSED-ESR SPECTROMETER THROUGH THE TIME DEPENDENCE OF THE POPULATION OF 1>AND ITS UNIQUE ELECTRON SPIN RESONANCE (ESR) SIGNATURE.

Description: STUDIES OF NET AND GROSS PRODUCTION IN THE SOUTHERN OCEAN: CONTROLS AND SCALING Studies of the biogeochemistry of the Southern Ocean are of great interest for several reasons. Upwelling of deep water supplies nutrients to the surface, causing summertime production to be high. The nutrient flux to the surface, as well as the character of regional ecosystems, may change as stratification and upwelling respond to global warming. Net production in the Southern Ocean removes nutrients from the upper waters. This process therefore determines the nutrient burden of Subantarctic Mode Waters, which supply nutrients to much of the extrapolar ocean (Sarmiento et al., 2004). The Southern Ocean is the world's largest high nutrient - low chlorophyll region. Because biogeochemical processes in HNLC waters from different regions share some common attributes, the Southern Ocean can serve as a model region for studying distributed phenomena. Finally, the cause of glacial-interglacial CO2 differences remains unresolved, but changes in Southern Ocean biogeochemistry remain a primary option for explaining these variations.

Description: MEASURMENTS, MODELING, AND ANYLYSES IN SUPPORT OF AURA AND OTHER NASA SATELLITE WITH AURA. In this study, we propose to investigate the H20 profile retrievals from AURA within the context of the precise and accurate - but geographically sparse high spectral resolution solar occultation observations from the Canadian ACE-FTS instrument. The aim of this investigation is to both evaluate the ACE and AURA retrievals by comparing coincident observations and to use additional information available from the occultation measurements to provide ancillary constraints on the physics and chemistry that determine the water vapor mixing ratio. In particular, we intend to retrieve from the ACE spectra profile information on HDO and other convective tracers in addition to H20 such as CO, 03, and HCCH. Combined with the global observations from AURA, these observations will provide a new view of the atmospheric hydrological cycle.

Description: MOIST PHYSICS DEVELOPMENT FOR GEOS-5 USING COLUMN MODELS WITH PARAMETERIZED DYNAMICS AGCMs exhibit a number of major, long-standing deficiencies which are at partly caused by inadequacies in their moist physics parameterization schemes. These deficiencies include an inability to correctly simulate most aspects of the tropical subseasonal oscillation in precipitation - the Madden-Julian Oscillation (MJO), and an inability to correctly simulate the seasonal means of tropical precipitation. The second problem is usually manifested by the existence of a so-called "double ITCZ" bias, which refers to the presence of an excessively ,strong Intertropical Convergence Zone (ITCZ) in the southern hemisphere. This bias exists in most current AGCMs (Meehl and Arblaster, 1998). In addition to these clearly manifested errors, AGCMs also exhibit a bewildering variety of sensitivities to parameters and to external orcings. A criticai area of uncertainty is in the response of the climate system to increases in C02 and other greenhouse gases. The major part of this uncertainty can be traced to the behavior of simulated clouds in AGCMs. Even AGCMs with similar net senstitivites to imposed ichanges in C02 can arrive at this sensitivity through very different combinations of cloud responses. This project will support on-going moist physics development for the GEOS-5 AGCM. Ultimately it aims to understand and alleviate biases in GEOS-5 due to problems in moist process parameterization. As part of this of this effort we plan to develop a Single Column Model (SCM) framework with parameterizes large-scal dyamics (SMC/PD).

Description: IMPLEMENTATION ISSUES AND VALIDATION OF SIGMA IN SPACE NETWORK ENVIRONMENT. There is significant interest in deploying the Internet protocol in space. A number of NASA-funded projects are studying the possible use of Internet technologies and protocols to support all aspects of data communication, including handover, with spacecraft. A spacecraft or a constellation of spacecrafts containing Earth observing sensing equipment form a sensor web which has to be handed off between ground stations. Consequently, researchers at NASA and University of Oklahoma are developing a new handover scheme, called Seamless IP-diversity based Generalized Mobility Architecture (SIGMA). Although the results from simulation and laboratory prototyping have shown very promising performance of SIGMA, its performance in the real space environment has yet to be studied. The objective of this project is to investigate a number of implementation issues of SIGMA for space missions, and evaluate SIGMA on an experimental satellite network to make it ready for space flight missions. Implementation issues to be investigated include survivability, scalability, power awareness, security, and networks in motion using simulation and laboratory prototype testbeds. Evaluation in an experimental satellite involves testing SIGMA (in conjunction with NASA, Cisco and Surrey Satellite Technologies) on the experimental UK-DMC (Disaster Monitoring Satellite). The results of this project will be directly applicable to a number of NASA projects involved in sensing the Earth's environment using Internet protocol in space. This is a three-year project with entry and exit TRLs of 315 and 516, respectively.

Sole Source Jusification: The purpose of this memorandum is to provide justification for procurement of a Real-Time Spectrum Analyzer manufactured by Tektronix, Inc.  A high-spped real-time spectrum analyzer is required in order to characterize performance of a Direct Readout System, which is being developed by Code 606.3.  This prototype design will serve as a baseline supporting remote sensing applications in scientific research as part of the EOS and NPP Programs.  A market survey of test equipment manufacturers between Tektronix, Anritsu and Rohde & Schwarz, was conducted in September 2006 that resulted in selecting the RSA6160A from Tektronix.  The RSA6106A is the only spectrum analyzer that is capable of characterizing and validating the Driect Readout System by analyzing signals in the range of 6GHz in real-time.  the data needs to be captured in real-time with live RF updates rates of 48,000 spectrums per second.  Additionally, the group will need the capability to capture data within a real-time capture bandwidth of 110MHz, with up to 1GB of acquisition memory, and the ability to observe frequency and amplitude changes over time.  To assist with pulse characterization, time-correlated measurements will be made across the frequency, time, and phase domins. And in order to maintain compatibility with existing hardware and to minimize manpower for adapting alternate solutions, this equipment must be purchased directly from Tektronix.  This is a one-time procurement in support of a unique NASA project established to represent a major breakthrough in processing remotely sensed spaceborne data.  And due to our unique funding constraints Tektronix has discounted the unit from $69.9K down to $50K, including freight. To elucidate the nature of the filament and the Vela X complex and their connection to the Vela pulsar, we propose spatially-resolved spectroscopy of the radio/X-ray filament with XIS. Simultaneously, we will measure the spectra of the Vela pulsar and PWN between 10 and 600 keV and perform phase-resolved spectroscopy of the pulsar in the 20-50 keV band.

Description: THE ROLE OF WATER IN THE EARLY FORMATION OF MARS: WET MAGMA OCEAN CRYSTALIZATION, THE GROWTH OF A WATER ATMOSPHERE, AND RETENTION OF WATER IN THE MANTLE Introduction: On Mars crater densities indicate that crust in both hemispheres dates from the early Noachian (e.g., Solomon et al., 1990; Frey et al., 2003)). Magnetized crustal provinces are further evidence for very ancient crustal formation (Acuna et al., 1999, Connerney et al., 1999). For Mars, our previous research indicates that the process of magma ocean fractional crystallization and subsequent mantle overturn is consistent with the formation of ancient crustal regions. On the Moon, magma ocean processes are thought to be responsible for the formation of the anorthitic highlands (Warren, 1985). If both the Martian and lunar earliest crusts were created by magma ocean processes, why does Mars lack a conspicuous plagioclase element? The Moon has likely been a completely dry body from its formation from heated material following the giant impact with the Earth (Hartman and David, 1975). Its shallow pressure range and dry composition both encourage plagioclase formation. Mars is known to have been a wetter planet in its past, and its high mantle iron content indicates more oxidizing initial conditions than were present on the Moon or Earth. Water in silicate melt suppresses plagioclase formation, and the higher pressure range of the Martian interior further limits its stability field. Water, then, may be one of the dominant variables in determining the outcomes of magma ocean crystallization and subsequent evolution of the terrestrial planets. Primary research areas: We propose to extend our magma ocean solidification and subsequent planetary evolution to the study of a wet magma ocean and its implications for creating an early steam atmosphere on Mars as well as a heterogeneously hydrous mantle with present-day implications for mantle viscosity, convective vigor, and magmatic source regions. These models make predications about the age and composition of the oldest Martian crust, about the compositions and ages of mantle reservoirs, and about the volumes and locations of water on the planet today. The proposed work should form an important link between theoretical modeling of early planetary formation and mission data from the planet today. Objectives: This proposal seeks funding for a three-year period, allowing work toward understanding the role of water in early planetary evolution that builds on the strong progress we have made to date (Elkins-Tanton et al., 2003; Elkins-Tanton and Parmentier, 2004). The three major proposed research areas are: 1. Applying models for magma ocean crystallization and overturn to a hydrous mantle composition, 2. Continuing work on the physics of crystallization of the magma ocean, and 3. Comparing predictions with surface and remote sensing data for Mars; and comparing predictions for Mars with those for other terrestrial planets, in particular, with the Earth and Moon.

Description: Reshaping Computer Engineering and Training for the Information Era While rapid advances in computer and networking technologies have dramatically changed the way of our life, the high education in our country has not fully exploited such technology advances in delivering high quality education and training. The limitations are reflected mainly in two aspects. First of all, traditional computer engineering (CE) curricula in most of universities in the country are CPU-centric (central processing unit) as it has been for the past few decades, ignoring the desperate need in the real world for computer engineers who have in depth knowledge of data communication and data storage technologies. Secondly, our engineering curriculum is still delivered in the traditional way in classrooms physically located on university campuses although high performance and low cost computers and the Internet are readily available. This is particularly true in computer engineering education and training where hands-on laboratory experiments and design projects are essential components of a CE curriculum. We propose here two innovative educational approaches to reshape the computer engineering education for the new information era.
