Description: TIMOTHY GIBLIN/THE COLLEGE OF CHARLESTONTHE TRANSITION FROM GAMMA-RAY BURST TO AFTERGLOWTHE TRANSIENT NATURE OF GAMMA-RAY BURSTS (GRBS) AND THE LIMITATIONS ENCOUNTERED IN DETECTING THEIR AFTERGLOWS HAVE MADE OBSERVATIONS OF THE TRANSITION FROM GRB TO AFTERGLOW ELUSIVE. HOWEVER, IN THE PAST DECADE, OBSERVATIONS OF BEPPOSSAX BURSTS AS WELL AS ARCHIVAL STUDIES OF BATSE DATA INDICATE A VARIETY OF POSSIBLE AFTERGLOW ONSET TIMES. IN SOME CASES THIS DELAY TIME IS SHORT (ON THE ORDER OF SECONDS), RESULTING IN CONTEMPORANEOUS PROMPT AND AFTERGLOW EMISSION, WHILE IN OTHER CASES THE DELAY TIME EXCEEDS THE BURST DURATION AND IS THEREFORE TEMPORALLY DECOUPLED FROM THE PROMPT BURST EMISSION. GIVEN THE SENSITIVITY OF SWIFT'S BAT AND XRT AT ENERGIES < 100 KEY, AFTERGLOW EMISSION MAY BE PREVELANT IN BURSTS AT THESE HIGH ENERGIES. THIS PROPOSAL AIMS TO UTILIZE THE BAT (AND XRT) DATA TO SEARCH FOR DISTINCT AND/OR ABRUPT SPECTRAL CHANGES DURING THE BURST THAT MAY BE ATTRIBUTED TO A SEPARATE UNDERLYING ORDELAYED EMISSION PHASE. IN THE INTERNAL/EXTERNAL SHOCK(ISIES) MODEL WE EXPECT AN EARLY TRANSITION FROM FAST TO SLOW COOLING, AS THE BREAK ENERGY (I.E. THE SYNCHROTRON SPECTRAL BREAK) PASSES THROUGH THE X-RAY BAND. ANALYSIS TOOLS INCLUDE TIME-DEPENDENT COLOR-COLOR DIAGRAMS TO PROBE SPECTRAL EVOLUTION PATTERNS. HARDNESS RATIOS WILL BE GENERATED BY BINNING THE BAT DATA TO PRODUCE HARD AND SOFTCOLOR INDICES. FURTHER, WE WILL FOLD THE REDSHIFTED AFTERGLOW SPECTRUM PREDICTED FROM THE EXTERNAL SHOCK THROUGH THE DETECTOR RESPONSE TO PREDICT THE EVOLUTION OF THE OBSERVED HARD AND SOFT COLORS. ONCE THE EMISSION COMPONENT IS IDENTIFIED, THE DELAY TIME WITH RESPECT TOTHE PROMPT EMISSION CAN BE DETERMINED. NOTE THAT FOR SOME BURSTS, THE OPTICAL AFTERGLOW (AND IN RARER CASES, POSSIBLY THE OPTICAL COUNTERPART) EMISSION WILL GREATLY AID IN CONSTRAINING THE AFTERGLOW DELAY TIME BY EXTRAPOLATING THE OPTICAL SPECTRUM TO THE X-RAY BAND TO DETERMINE IF THEY ARE THE ONE-IN-THE-SAME EMISSION COMPONENT. THIS IS NOT EXPECTED TO BE THE CASE IF THE OPTICAL EMISSION IS DUE TO THE REVERSE SHOCK IN THE ISLES MODEL. WE PROPOSE TO ANALYZE THE EXISTING SWIFT DATASET AS WELL AS BURSTS THAT ARE OBSERVED THROUGHOUT THE DURATION OF THE MISSION. OUR FINAL GOAL IS TO ESTABLISH A STATISTICAL SAMPLE OF DELAY TIMES AND AFTERGLOW SPECTRAL PROPERTIES AT HIGH-ENERGIES THAT CAN BE COLLECTIVELY STUDIED WITH OTHER BURST PROPERTIES. THIS WILL PLAYA CRUCIAL IN OUR UNDERSTANDING OF THE ENVIRONMENT AND ENERGETICS OF THE COLLAPSAR PROGENITOR. WE REQUEST FUNDING FOR ONE YEAR TO DEVELOP THE ANALYSIS TOOLS AND ANALYZE THE FIRST TWELVE MONTHS OF BAT AND XRT BURST DATA ACCUMULATED BY SWIFT. THE NECESSARY ANALYSIS TOOLS WILL THEN BE IN PLACE FOR US TO ANALYZE FUTURE SWIFT DATA AS IT BECOMES READILY AVAILABLE FOR EACH BURST.

Description: PLANETS AND SATELLITES SOUTHWEST RESEARCH INSTITUTE THIS PROPOSAL CONTAINS FOUR TASKS CONCERNING THE EARLY EVOLUTION OF THE OUTER SOLAR SYSTEM. TASK 1 EXAMINES THE EVOLUTION OF A PROTOSATELLITE DISK ORBITING A GROWING GAS PLANET, IN PARTICULAR ITS IMPLICATIONS FOR THE CONFIGURATIONS, MASSES AND COMPOSITIONS OF RESULTING REGULAR SATELLITE SYSTEM. THE OBJECTIVE IS TO MODEL THE FORMATION OF JUPITER'S GALILEAN SATELLITES FROM A GAS-STRAVED CIRCUMPLANETARY ACCRETION DISK WITHIN THE CONTEXT OF THE EARLIEST EVOLUTION OF THE PLANET ITSELF, AND TO ASSESS THE POSSIBILITY THAT EARLIER GENERATIONS OF SATELLITES MAY HAVE FORMED BUT BEEN LOST THROUGH DISK INTERACTIONS. TASK 2 ADDRESSES SEVERAL ASPECTS OF THE SATURNIAN SATELLITE SYSTEM AND THE DOMINANCE OF THIS SYSTEMS TOTAL MASS BY A SINGLE SATELLITE, TITAN. WE PROPOSE TO EVALUTE THE POTENTIAL FOR TITAN TO BE LEFT AS A SOLE LARGE SATELLITE DUE TO ITS ABILITY TO OPEN A GAP IN ITS PROTOSATELLITE DISK, AND TO INVESTIGATE WHETHER RELATED DISK INTERACTIONS COULD ACCOUNT FOR TITAN'S CURRENT ECCENTRICITY AND THE LARGE INCLINATION OF LAPETUS. TASK 3 CONSIDERS THE EARLY ORBITAL MIGRATIONS OF JUPITER AND SATURN THEMSELVES DURING THE DISPERSAL OF THE SOLAR NEBULA. TASK 4 CONCENTRATES ON WHAT HAS BEEN AN ONGOING CHALLENGE TO PLANET FORMATION MODELS; FORMING THE ICE-GIANTS URANUS AND NEPTUNE AT DISTANCES FROM THE SUN WHERE MATERIAL CAN EASILY BE SCATTERED OUT OF THE SOLAR SYSTEM BEFORE BEING ACCRETED. HERE WE EXPLORE A RUNAWAY MODE OF IN-SITU ACCRETION THAT MAY HAVE BEEN POSSIBLE DUR TO ACOUSTIC WAVE DAMPING OF EMBRYO ECCENTRICITIES BY A SMALL, DISSIPATING REMNANT OF THE SOLAR NEBULA.

Description: "OPTIMUM BAND SELECTION TECHNIQUES UNDER HYPERSPECTRAL IMAGE ANALYSIS FOR MATERIAL IDENTIFICATION AND CLASSIFICATION"THE COMPLEXITY INVOLVED IN COLLECTING, STORING, ANALYSIS AND PROCESSING OF VOLUMINOUS REMOTE SENSING MULTI-DIMENSIONAL DATA FOR AN ARRAY OF "EARTH SYSTEM SCIENCE" APPLICATIONS IS A WELL KNOWN PROBLEM TO NASA. THE RECENT HYPERSPECTRAL IMAGING (HSI) TECHNOLOGY HAVE EVOLVED FROM ITS EARLIER VERSION OF MULTISPECTRAL IMAGING (MSI). IN HSI, IMAGES ARE ACQUIRED USING HUNDREDS OF SPECTRAL CHANNELS WHEN COMPARED TO FEWER CHANNELS IN MSI. HOWEVER, OVER THE YEARS THERE HAS NOT BEEN MUCH SIGNIFICANT DEVELOPMENT OF PROCESSING ALGORITHMS FOR THESE EVER GROWING (IN THE SPECTRAL DIRECTION) ELECTRO-OPTICAL DATA SETS. THE NEED TO COME UP WITH INTELLIGENT BAND SELECTION TECHNIQUES IS EVEN STRONGER SINCE WE ARE MOVING IN TO THE ERA OF ULTRASPECTRAL IMAGING (USI). THE USI TECHNOLOGY USUALLY CONSISTS OF MEASUREMENTS TAKEN IN THOUSANDS OF SPECTRAL CHANNELS. IN ALL THREE IMAGING TECHNOLOGIES, EACH SPATIAL PIXEL IS TREATED AS A COLUMN VECTOR THAT CONTAINS SPECTRAL INFORMATION FROM EACH CHANNEL. DUE TO THE EVER GROWING HIGHER SPECTRAL DIMENSIONALITY OF THE REMOTE SENSING DATA, EACH IMAGE PIXEL VECTOR POSSESSES MORE INFORMATION THAN EVER BEFORE. HOWEVER, DUE TO NOISE AND OTHER UNAVOIDABLE ATMOSPHERIC INTERFERENCE, A PURE SIGNATURE FOR A CLASS KNOWN AS THE END-MEMBER MAY BE REPRESENTED BY A MIXTURE OR COMBINATION OF SPECTRAL SIGNATURE FROM NEIGHBORING PIXELS. TO ENCAPSULATE THE UNCERTAINTY CREATED BY A PIXEL VECTOR DUE TO NOISE AND OTHER INTERFERENCE DEMANDS A STOCHASTIC TREATMENT. THIS PROPOSAL FOCUSES ON DERIVING CLASSIFICATION AND TARGET DETECTION METHODS BASED ON NON-TRANSFORMED DATA. THE INTENT IS THAT WITHOUT THE COST OF THE DECORRELATING TRANSFORM, THAT THE DERIVED CLASSIFICATION ALGORITHMS WILL HAVE SUITABLE COMPLEXITY FOR USE IN PRACTICAL CLASSIFICATION SYSTEMS. EARLIER RESEARCH HAS INVESTIGATED USING A REDUCED COLOR SPACE FOR IMPLEMENTING MATERIAL CLASSIFICATION OFHSI DATA. THIS "BEST BAND" SELECTION (BBS) METHOD RELIES SOLELY ON THE DETERMINISTIC DISTANCE MEASURES OF MINIMUM EUCLIDEAN DISTANCE AND SPECTRAL ANGLE MAPPER. THE RESULTS OF THIS RESEARCH WERE ALGORITHMS THAT GAVEENHANCED CLASS SEPARATION USING A REDUCED NUMBER OF SPECTRAL COLOR BANDS. OUR CURRENT RESEARCH EXTENDS THE OPTIMUM BAND SELECTION TECHNIQUES IN TWO SEPARATE DIRECTIONS. THE FIRST IS TO EXTEND THE BBS RESULTS TO STOCHASTIC DISTANCE METRICS SUCH AS HIDDEN MARKOV AND LEIBLER-KULLBACK MEASURES. STUDIES HAVE SHOWN THAT THE STOCHASTIC DISTANCE MEASURES CAN RESULT IN IMPROVED CLASSIFICATION PERFORMANCE RELATIVE TO DETERMINISTIC METRICS. TO DATE, THE PROBLEM OF BEST BAND SELECTION USING STOCHASTIC METRICS HAS NOT BEEN ADDRESSED IN THE LITERATURE. THE ISSUE OF STOCHASTIC MEASURES FOR BBS WILL BE THE PRIMARY FOCUS OF THE PROPOSED RESEARCH. THE SECOND DIRECTION FOR EXTENDING BEST BAND SELECTION IS IN INCORPORATING SENSOR MODELS OF HSI DATA COLLECTION INTO THE BBS ALGORITHM. WE WILL SPECIFICALLY EXTEND THE BBS METHOD USING DERIVED ANALYTICAL MODELS OF SPECTRAL PROFILES.

Description: "STUDY OF TIBETAN PLATEAU WITH MODIS, TRMM DATA" The Tibetan Plateau plays important roles in determining the formation and varation of regional weather and climate in east and south Asia, as well as atmospheric circulation in the Northern Hemisphere in general.  However, the study of climatic impact of Tibetan Plateau has been relatively limited in the past.  This is partly due to lack of the remotely sensed observational data over the Tibetan Plateau, and also because of the difficulties in exchanging the data between Chinese and western scholars.  With this fellowship proposal, we plan to undertake a first research effort to integrate multi-year (2000-present)NASA MODIS snow cover and TRMM rainfall data with in situ Chineses station data, including the snow data from 60 Chineses ground-observing snow stations over the Tibetan Plateau and 2200 ground-based meteorological stations over Chinese continent, to achieve the following research components:  1) Evaluate the MODIS snow cover estimates and in situ Chinese ground-based snow stations over the Tibetan Plateau.  2)  Incorporate MODIS snow cover estimates and in situ Chinese ground-based snow station data to obtain a database with multi-year winter snow cover and depth over the Tibetan Plateau.  3)  Integrate the obtained multi-year winter snow database with TRMM precipitation estimates (cover global tropics and sub-tropics) and 2200 ground-based Chinese meteorological station data to study the relationship between the Tibetan winter (November to February) snow cover and Asian summer (June to August) precipitation.  4)  Assimilate the snow data into state-of-the-art Community Climate System model (CCSM) to further study the impact of winter Tibetan snow cover on Asian summer precipitation.  Specific attention will be paid to general circulation associated with Asian monsoon activities.  In addition, we will further explore impact of Tibetan snow cover on the global atmospheric circulation in general.  The possible relationship between Tibetan snow cover on Northern American atmospheric circulation will be specifically investigated.  It is anticipated the study from this proposed activities could fill gaps of our knowledge regarding to the weather and climate impact from the Tibetan Plateau.

Description: JOINT GEO-INFORMATICS LABORATORY- PHASE II (JGIL) ABSTRACT: George Mason University's Laboratory for Advanced Information Technologies and Standards (LAITS) had successfully completed the phase I cooperation with NASA Goddard Space Flight Center for the Joint Geo-Informatics Laboratory (JGIL-I). In this proposal, GMU's Center for Spatial Information Science and Systems (CSISS), which LAITS is part of, proposes to enter the second-phase cooperation for the Joint Geo-Informatics Laboratory (JGIL) with NASA Goddard Space Flight Center. The performance period for the proposed cooperation will be three years starting July 1, 2006. JGIL will conduct information technology research, prototyping, system development in support of NASA Code 610.2 and other laboratories at Goddard Space Flight Center related to applying information technologies to Earth and space sciences. General categories of JGIL projects fall within but not limited to the following categories: research and development in geo-information theory and technology; prototypes of geospatial data, information, knowledge, decision-supporting, and modeling systems; science data, information products and services; development and support of operational data and information systems; development and implementation of geo-informatic standards; scientific and technical support to NASA's international and national commitments and activities; research in other disciplines (e.g., space and planetary sciences) that can use the technology and systems developed by or experiences and knowledge of JGIL. Although the initial project of JGIL-II has been identified and described in this agreement, additional projects of JGIL will be added into the cooperative agreement during the performance period of this, agreement as argumentations, depending on successfully securing funds by JGIL researchers (both GMU and GSFC researchers) through solicited and un-solicited proposals.

Description: QUANTITATIVE ANALYSIS OF THE DEFORMATIONAL HISTORY AND TIMING OF THE SIERRA MADERAL IMPACT STRUCTURE, WEST TEXAS Funding is requested for a detailed geologic study the Sierra Madera impact crater in west Texas. This crater was last studied in the 1960's and is an excellent site for the proposed research because it is a complex crater that formed in well-studied Permian Basin stratigraphy, the crater is weil exposed and it was not subjected to subsequent deformation. The proposed research has the following objectives: 1) to map, describe and sample macroscopic deformation features (e.g. shattercones, breccias, dikes, sills, etc.) as well as describe, document and analyze microscopic deformation features within this crater; 2) to quantitatively determine the amount of shock deformation recorded at Sierra Madera; and 3) to determine the age of this impact event through fission-track analysis and (U-Th)/He thermochronoIogy. We propose to characterize the modes of deformation of the Sicrra Madera crater and quantitativelly determine its deformation history by integrating geologic mapping, microscopy, and analytical methods. First, we will map the distribution and geometries of macroscopic shock induced features (shattercones and breccias) in outcrops and in the subsurface. Microscopic deformation in these features (e.g. planar elements, twinning, fracturing and evidence of metamorphic reactions) will be characterized petrographically. Lastly, XRD, FTIFt, SEM and oil immersion-spindle stage analyses of quartz and calcite in breccias and shattercones will provide a quantitative measure of the pressure history. Quartz deformation features produced at known pressures and temperatures will be compared to coeval calcite samples to generate a calcite deformation scale, which should be applicable to impact craters in quartz-free sedimentary rocks. Well-studied craters in carbonate host rocks include small diameter craters (Meteor Crater,<2 km and Steinheirn, -3.8 km) and large diameter craters (Ries and Haughton, both 24 km). It is apparent there is a gap in deformational studies of carbonate impact structures based on crater diameter. The Sierra Madera impact structure with a diameter of 12.9 km will provide data in a critical intermediate size range, where data currently is lacking. The age of the Sierra Madera impact event will be determined by fission-track analysis and (U-Th)Me thermochronoiogy of apatite and zircon in Permian and Cretaceous sandstone samples in the crater. If successful these low-temperature techniques may provide a useful method to more precisely determine the age of many impact craters, especially those where the meteorite itself is not preserved. The proposed study of the Sierra Madera impact crater will provide an excellent terrestrial analog for studying extraterrestrial craters in current and future NASA missions. Furthermore, an enhanced understanding of the Sierra Madera impact crater will provide a baseline fur future studies of rock and mineral deformation history and dating of both terrestrial and planetary craters.

Description: INTERPRETATION OF MARTIAN POLAR STRATIGRAPHY USING ICE FLOW INVERSE MODELING How flow and mass balance shape the Martian ice caps, and whether subglacial melting ever occurs, are fundamental questions for exploring and understanding Mars. These questions can be addressed directly and quantitatively by using inverse modeling to interpret observed ice cap stratigraphy and topography. Inverse modeling estimates ice cap variables and climatic forcing by assimilating observations with a rigorous, though judiciously limited, physical model. (Forward modeling, by contrast, specifies parameters in a comprehensive physical model and is driven by specified climate forcing to predict ice cap characteristics.) Data interpretation using inverse modeling has yielded, for example, the discovery of high basal melt rates beneath the Greenland ice cap, where no melting at all had been expected. Such interpretation has yet to be applied to the Martian polar layered deposits (PLD), but it is now timely to do so: Topographic data and imagery to map exposed strata now densely cover the PLD, and we are about to get our first look at basal topography and stratigraphy inside the ice from orbital sounding radars. The University of Washington glaciology group has longstanding expertise in combining observations with ice flow inverse modeling to probe terrestrial ice caps. We propose to combine this expertise with Caltech's long specialization in Mars polar studies, to discriminate mass balance from flow processes on Mars, and to probe for evidence of basal melting that might be recorded within the Martian PLD. Specifically, we aim to address the following questions: (1) Does stratigraphy in the north or south PLD display unambiguous evidence for equilibration by large-scale ice flow, now or in the past? (2) Is there evidence for basal sliding, and thus possible subglacial water? In particular, does ice near complex features such as chasmae show evidence of local flow or basal melting, in the past if not now? (3) What are the regional- to large-scale spatial patterns of accumulation and ablation? By basing our data interpretation on the physical models inherent in the flow inverse method, we will make optimal use of partial or fragmentary observations. The imminent observations of basal topography and internal layering from the MARSIS radar will thus, via this method, provide exceptional insight into past and present ice dynamics on Mars.

Description: LOWENERGY PLANTETARY EXCAVATOR (LPE) SBIR PHASE II LOW-ENERGY PLANETARY EXCAVATOR (LPE) PROTOTYPE SBIR CONTRACT  ORBITEC PROPOSES TO DEVELOP AN INNOVATIVE LOW-ENERGY PLANETARY EXCAVATOR (LPE) TO EXCAVATE IN SITU REGOLITH, ICEREGOLITH MIXTURES, AND A VARIETY OF OTHER GEOLOGIC MATERIALS TO SUPPORT FUTURE ACTIVITIES ON THE MOON AND MARS. THE LPE UTILIZES AN INNOVATIVE CUTTERHEAD TO EFFICIENTLY EXCAVATE A WIDE RANGE OF DIFFERENT PLANETARY SURFACE MATERIALS. CURRENT MECHANICAL EXCAVATORS OPERATES EFFICIENTLY ONLY IN A NARROW RANGE OF MATERIAL CONDITIONS. THE LPE WILL SENSE GEOLOGIC CHANGES AND RESPOND WITH CHANGES IN THE CUTTERHEAD TO ACHIEVE THE LOWEST CUTTING ENERGY POSSIBLE. THE RESULT IS A FLEXIBLE MACHINE WITH REDUCED POWER AND MASS REQUIREMENTS. THE PHASE II LPE PROTOTYPE UNIT IS DESIGNED TO BE A TESTBED TO EVALUATE THE PERFORMANCE OF THE VARIABLE GEOMETRY CUTTERHEAD IN SIMULATED LUNAR ICE-REGOLITH MATERIAL. IT IS NOT DESIGNED TO BE A FULLY-FUNCTIONAL EXCAVATOR. THE CUTTERHEAD IS THE KEY DESIGN DRIVER FOR THE REST OF THE EXCAVATOR. THE REST OF THE EXCAVATOR MUST SUPPLY THE THRUST AND TORQUE REQUIRED TO CAUSE FAILURES IN THE TARGET MATERIAL. THE MAJOR COMPONENTS OF THE LPE PROTOTYPE UNIT ARE THE CUTTERHEAD ASSEMBLY, THE TRANSLATION STAGE, AND THE SUPPORT FRAME. THE CUTTERHEAD ASSEMBLY CONTAINS ELECTRIC DRIVE MOTORS THAT ROTATE THE CUTTERHEAD, LINEAR ACTUATORS THAT CONTROL THE SUMPING DEPTH (DISTANCE OF THE CUTTERHEAD INTO THE EXCAVATED MATERIAL), LINEAR ACTUATORS THAT CONTROL THE CUTTERHEAD GEOMETRY, AND A MOUNTING BLOCK. THE TRANSLATION STAGE CONSISTS OF A LEAD SCREW AND AN ELECTRIC LEAD SCREW DRIVE MOTOR. THE SUPPORT FRAME CONSISTS OF TWO HORIZONTAL GUIDE RAILS AND THE SUPPORT STANDS.  DURING OPERATION, THE LEAD SCREW MOVES THE CUTTERHEAD ASSEMBLY ALONG THE GUIDE RAILS AND PROVIDES THE FORWARD THRUST ON THE CUTTERHEAD. NOTE THAT THE SUPPORT STANDS WOULD NEED TO BE ATTACHED TO THE FLOOR BEFORE OPERATION. TECHNICAL OBJECTIVES THE PRIMARY OBJECTIVE OF THE PHASE II EFFORT WILL BE TO DESIGN, BUILD, TEST, AND DELIVER AN OPERATIONAL LPE PROTOTYPE UNIT TO NASA.  THE SPECIFIC TECHNICAL OBJECTIVES OF THE PHASE II EFFORT WOULD INCLUDE:   REFINE THE SYSTEM REQUIREMENTS FOR THE LPE PROTOTYPE UNIT, A PHASE III TECHNOLOGY DEMONSTRATION UNIT, AND A LPE PRODUCTION UNIT;   DETERMINE THE RANGE OF POTENTIAL ICE-REGOLITH MECHANICAL PROPERTIES EXPECTED ON THE MOON;   IDENTIFY AND DEVELOP EFFECTIVE MECHANICAL SIMULANTS THAT ARE AS CLOSE TO TRUE LUNAR CONDITIONS AS POSSIBLE;   DESIGN AND ANALYZE A LPE PROTOTYPE UNIT;   CONSTRUCT A COMPUTERIZED PERFORMANCE PREDICTION MODEL FOR THE CUTTERHEAD AND EXCAVATION MACHINE;   BUILD AND TEST THE LPE PROTOTYPE UNIT;   DELIVER THE LPE PROTOTYPE UNIT TO NASA AND DEMONSTRATE ITS OPERATION;   DEVELOP CONCEPTUAL DESIGNS FOR A PHASE III LPE TECHNOLOGY DEMONSTRATION UNIT AND A LPE PRODUCTION UNIT. WORK PLAN 1) REFINE THE LPE SYSTEM REQUIREMENTS, 2) DETERMINE THE POTENTIAL ICE-REGOLITH PROPERTIES, 3) DEVELOP AN ICE-REGOLITH SIMULANT FOR LPE PROTOTYPE TESTING, 4) LPE DESIGN AND ANALYSIS, 5) LPE PROTOTYPE DEVELOPMENT AND FABRICATION, 6) LPE PROTOTYPE TESTING AND DATA ANALYSIS, 7) LPE PROTOTYPE DELIVERY TO NASA, 8) LPE TECHNOLOGY DEMONSTRATION UNIT, 9) LPE PRODUCTION UNIT, AND 10) PROJECT MANAGEMENT & REPORTING.

Description: Using Intelligent Agents to Form a Sensor Web for Autonomous Mission Operations ABSTRACT: Our team proposes to develop an architecture which shifts sensor web control to a distributed set of intelligent agents versus a centrally controlled architecture. Constellation missions introduce levels of complexity that are not easily maintained by a central management activity. A network of intelligent agents reduces management requirements by making use of model based system prediction, and autonomic model/agent collaboration. The proposed architecture incorporates agents distributed throughout the operational environment that monitor and manage spacecraft systems and self-manage the sensor web system via peer-to-peer collaboration. The intelligent agents are mobile and thus will be able to traverse between on-orbit and ground based systems. This network of intelligent mobile agents will be capable of modeling the future behavior of the subsystems and components that they are assigned to. Using situational awareness, the agents will be able.to negotiate activities to self-optimize their subsystems or component. Furthermore, presented with a set of system goals, the network of agents will collaborate within the system to arbitrate the best set of proposed three (3) year effort to an end result proof of concept demonstration, at TRL 7. The demonstration will exercise the architectural features and prove applicability across a broad spectrum of Earth Science missions. Building on the team's experience with EO-1 and ST-5, the new demonstration will take steps towards increased levels of autonomy in mission operations.

Description: NASA SPONSORED CLASSROOM OF THE FUTURE During the last decade the Center for Educational Technologies' project, CLASSROOM OF THE FUTURE, has worked closely with NASA Education to explore and develop new tools to improve science teaching and learning with technology. In 2006 COTF proposes to build on recently successful activities and to develop innovations for continual advancements in technology applied to education. The main tasks are (1) convert the Virtual Design Center, evaluations and various web design skills into an educational curriculum development service; (2) Inspiration research to continue understanding the measurement and enhancement of inspiration; (3) Earthispace educator professional development to satisfy a need for increased for training for NASA and other informal educators; (4) LunarWorld: education, research and SIM to develop educational tools to accompany humanity's second foray beyond Earth orbit; (5) NASA's career central to consolidate dispersed career information; (6) Educational technology exploration lab to continue COTF's mandate to be on the leading edge of applications of new technology to education; (7) NASA educational television to assist NASA in program scheduling and planning; and (8) Educational Outreach to continue to represent NASA to teachers through the upper Ohio valley. All of these efforts build on NASA's current and developing exploration and education interests, including the generational movement to the Moon, and development of educational uses for new technologies such as video podcasting.
